```{r report-setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)

# Several model files name their first chunk "setup". Allow the duplicate
# labels so they can all be knitted into this one report.
options(knitr.duplicate.label = "allow")

# knit_module(): knits one numbered file INTO this report.
# Each file has its own YAML header (so it can be knit alone); we strip that
# header off so this report keeps a single title and table of contents.
# A file that is missing or still empty shows a short placeholder instead.
knit_module <- function(file) {
  placeholder <- "*This section is still in progress and will be added when the model is finished.*"
  if (!file.exists(file)) { cat(placeholder); return(invisible()) }
  lines    <- readLines(file, warn = FALSE)
  yaml_end <- which(trimws(lines) == "---")[2]          # line where the YAML header ends
  body     <- if (is.na(yaml_end)) lines else lines[-(1:yaml_end)]
  if (!any(nzchar(trimws(body)))) { cat(placeholder); return(invisible()) }
  out <- knitr::knit_child(text = body, envir = globalenv(), quiet = TRUE)
  cat(out, sep = "\n")
}

```

# 1. Introduction and Problem Statement

```{r intro-data}
raw <- read.csv("song_longevity.csv", stringsAsFactors = TRUE)
```

## The situation

A record label releases far more songs than it can afford to promote. Marketing budget, playlist pitching and social-media pushes have to be rationed, and most releases never become hits. Our data has `r format(nrow(raw), big.mark = ",")` songs with their audio features (energy, danceability, tempo...), label and marketing information, early streaming and social signals, and whether each song became a hit. The question for this analysis is:

> **Can we accurately predict which songs will become hits?**

## Who this is for

The audience is a record label's **A&R and marketing team**. They decide which new releases get the marketing push. Pushing a song that goes nowhere wastes budget, and failing to back a song that would have been a hit gives up the most valuable outcome the label has. A model that flags the songs most likely to become hits lets the team put its budget behind them.

## How we judge the models

Only `r round(100 * mean(raw$is_hit == 1))`% of songs are hits. A "model" that predicts *no song is ever a hit* is already `r round(100 * mean(raw$is_hit == 0))`% accurate while being useless to the label, so accuracy alone is misleading. We judge every model by **Kappa**, which measures agreement between the predictions and the truth beyond what chance alone would give. Each confusion matrix also reports the two kinds of mistake:

* **False negative (missed hit):** the model says "not a hit", but the song became a hit. The label did not back it.
* **False positive (false alarm):** the model says "hit", but the song did not become one. The label spent budget on it.

## Approach

All models use the same 50/50 split into training and test songs. We start with K-means clustering to understand the types of songs and promotion strategies in the data. We then build and try to improve six individual models: logistic regression, KNN, an artificial neural network (ANN), a support vector machine (SVM), a decision tree and a random forest. Their predictions then become the inputs to a second-level decision tree: a **stacked model**, or "model of models". The final sections compare all the models and translate the results into dollars for the label.

# 11. Comparing the Models

```{r compare}
library(caret)

# Each model's final confusion matrix on the test songs. We use its saved rds
# file when there is one, otherwise the confusion matrix it left in the
# workspace when its section was knitted above. Unfinished models are skipped.
models <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Logistic Regression", "KNN", "ANN", "SVM", "Decision Tree", "Random Forest", "Stacked Model"),
  file  = c("cm_lr", "cm_knn", "cm_ann", "cm_svm", "cm_dt", "cm_rf", "cm_stacked")
)

get_cm <- function(name) {
  path <- file.path("rds", paste0(name, ".rds"))
  if (file.exists(path)) return(readRDS(path))
  if (exists(name, envir = globalenv())) return(get(name, envir = globalenv()))
  NULL
}

cms <- setNames(lapply(models$file, get_cm), models$Model)
cms <- cms[!sapply(cms, is.null)]                    # keep only finished models

compare <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(cms), function(m) {
  cm <- cms[[m]]
  data.frame(Model       = m,
             Kappa       = round(unname(cm$overall["Kappa"]), 3),
             Accuracy    = round(unname(cm$overall["Accuracy"]), 3),
             Sensitivity = round(unname(cm$byClass["Sensitivity"]), 3),
             Specificity = round(unname(cm$byClass["Specificity"]), 3),
             Hits_caught = cm$table["1", "1"],         # predicted hit, was a hit
             Missed_hits = cm$table["0", "1"],         # predicted not a hit, was a hit
             False_alarms = cm$table["1", "0"])        # predicted hit, was not a hit
}))
compare <- compare[order(-compare$Kappa), ]

knitr::kable(compare, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Model", "Kappa", "Accuracy", "Sensitivity", "Specificity",
                           "Hits caught", "Missed hits", "False alarms"),
             caption = "Every finished model on the test songs, best Kappa first")

best      <- compare[1, ]
n_test    <- sum(cms[[1]]$table)                     # number of test songs
n_hits    <- sum(cms[[1]]$table[, "1"])              # hits among them
missing   <- setdiff(models$Model, compare$Model)
```

The best model so far is **`r best$Model`** with a Kappa of `r best$Kappa`. Of the `r format(n_hits, big.mark = ",")` hits among the `r format(n_test, big.mark = ",")` test songs, it catches `r format(best$Hits_caught, big.mark = ",")` (`r round(100 * best$Sensitivity)`%) and raises `r format(best$False_alarms, big.mark = ",")` false alarms.
`r if (length(missing) > 0) paste0("*Not yet in this table: ", paste(missing, collapse = ", "), ".*")`
